problems.description: Module-level `init_db()` now executes as an import side effect using whatever DATABASE is set at import time; the test fixture has to work around this with importlib.reload + env override, where an app-factory or lazy-init pattern would be cleaner.
Test isolation relies on importlib.reload(app_module) plus a DATABASE env override; functional and isolated, but couples the suite to module import order and reload semantics.

The measured 0.68 convention score is dominated by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py) plus a pre-existing app.py class-naming issue; this diff's additions introduce zero new violations.

strengths: Fixes a real behavioral bug: new tasks were created with status 'done' and are now correctly created as 'pending'.
Thorough 13-test suite covering CRUD happy paths, validation errors (missing/blank title, no body), not-found cases, ordering, and a dedicated regression test pinning the status default.
Clean per-test DB isolation via tempfile-backed DATABASE override with no cross-test contamination.
Zero new SonarQube findings (bugs/smells/complexity/duplications all +0) and no new convention violations in the diff; parameterized SQL and existing get_db/init_db helpers preserved.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid greenfield session that fixes the create-task default-status bug and adds a comprehensive, well-isolated test suite with no new SonarQube or convention findings — the measured 0.68 convention score is inflated by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touches.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded dev secret; tokens are forgeable if the env var is unset in any non-dev deployment.
require_auth sets request.user on the Flask request proxy instead of the idiomatic flask.g application-context object.
create_task still uses the deprecated datetime.utcnow() even though the module now imports timezone and generate_token uses datetime.now(timezone.utc) — inconsistent timestamp handling.
fetch_task, documented as an alias for legacy clients, now requires a mandatory owner_id positional arg, silently breaking the legacy call contract it exists to serve.
No tests accompany the +27 functions covering register/login/token verification and owner scoping.
Login endpoint has no rate limiting or lockout, leaving credential brute force unmitigated.
SonarQube delta shows cognitive complexity +16 and one new smell on the 369-line addition — the require_auth wrapper and owner_id threading add real branching weight.

strengths: Passwords stored as werkzeug hashes, never plaintext
Parameterized SQL throughout list/get/update — no injection surface introduced
owner_id scoped on every read and write, preventing cross-user IDOR
Idempotent PRAGMA-based migration adds owner_id to pre-existing tasks tables
JWT uses sub + exp with UTC time; @wraps preserves view function metadata
Respects the codebase's flat-module layout, section-comment style, and type-hinted signature conventions
commit_reviews.summary: A security-conscious feature addition (hashed auth + per-owner scoping) that fits the app's existing structure and genuinely improves it, though it ships modest debt — request.user instead of flask.g, deprecated utcnow, an unversioned legacy alias signature, and no tests — and its clean diff sits inside a repo that already measures 0.68 convention compliance, with most listed violations (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py) in files this commit never touches, so the 0.68 overstates this change's own deviation.

problems.description: _notify_admin remains a dead 'Stub — not yet wired' that duplicates the notification concern; two competing notification channels now coexist with no deprecation note.
Test fixture uses importlib.reload(app_module) per test to reset the module-level init_db()/DATABASE state — works, but couples tests to import mechanics and can hide cross-test leakage.

The measured 23 convention violations are largely analyzer false positives: lowercase celery_app/broker_url/result_backend/task_serializer are the documented Celery conventions, not constant-naming violations.
Fallback to '{username}@example.com' fabricates recipients for users with no email on file, which can silently queue mail to non-existent addresses.

strengths: Async notification via Celery with .delay() wrapped in try/except so a broker outage can never fail the API response — fire-and-forget done correctly.
Correct edge handling: notification only fires on a genuine status transition (previous is not None and previous['status'] != 'completed').
DB migration mirrors the existing owner_id pattern (idempotent PRAGMA + ALTER TABLE guard) and extends create_user/register cleanly with an optional email.
celery_app split from app.py so the worker can import without pulling in Flask, with env-overridable broker/backend URLs.
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally sound integration session that wires a real async notification path (Celery on the story's 6379 Redis) with good failure-guard and transition-handling; I flag a discrepancy where the 0.68 convention score stems from analyzer false positives on Celery's lowercase-config conventions rather than real style breaks.

problems.description: BaseRepository interpolates self.table_name into SQL via f-string (SELECT/DELETE). Safe today only because table_name is a static class attribute; the pattern is a latent injection hazard if any subclass ever assigns a dynamic value.

task_repository/user_repository are instantiated at module import time bound to the DATABASE constant, coupling DB access to import side-effects and making the app hard to test without dependency injection.
Abstract methods in BaseRepository use bare '...' ellipsis bodies; a docstring or explicit NotImplementedError would better communicate the contract.
No tests accompany the new repository layer — a pure refactor of CRUD logic is exactly the case where a coverage guard should be added.

strengths: Centralizes all SQLite access into a dedicated repositories/ package with a clean ABC (BaseRepository) and typed subclasses.
Net -89 lines: removes substantial duplicated connection/CRUD boilerplate from app.py.
Table-creation and migration logic consolidated into create_table(), replacing the inline PRAGMA-driven migrations.
New code follows conventions consistently — PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, type hints, docstrings, and a proper __init__ re-export.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid layering refactor that moves all SQLite access behind a clean repository ABC and cuts ~89 lines of duplication from app.py, with the only real caveats being minor (f-string table-name interpolation, import-time singletons) and the low 0.68 convention score reflecting pre-existing violations in celery_app.py/celery_config.py that this commit does not touch.

problems.description: get_tasks_page runs a full COUNT(*) via count_by_owner on every paginated request — an O(n) scan per page that partially undercuts the scalability benefit of cursor pagination.

Cognitive complexity +37 (SonarQube) from nested cursor/limit validation in list_tasks and the try/except+decode chain in rate_limit_key; the param-parsing branches could be extracted into a small helper.

The Flask app now hard-requires a reachable Redis at startup for Flask-Limiter storage (default redis://localhost:6379); if Redis is down, serving fails rather than degrading. Consistent with the story's existing celery+redis usage, but a new availability coupling for the web tier.
The client fixture mutates global os.environ and importlib.reload()s app per test — an existing fragile pattern, now extended to REDIS_URL. Functional but order-dependent in larger suites.

Measured convention score is 0.68 with 23 violations, but the cited violations (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE) are in files this commit does NOT touch — pre-existing repo debt, not introduced here.

strengths: Correct cursor-based pagination: fetch limit+1 rows to derive has_more, then trim — the canonical stable-key pagination pattern over the O(n) offset approach.
rate_limit_key keys by authenticated user id with client-IP fallback, correctly avoiding both brute-force bypass and cross-user starvation behind a proxy.
Pagination params are validated with bounded limits (MAX_PAGE_LIMIT=100) and clean 400 JSON errors; the dedicated 429 errorhandler keeps the API's error contract uniform.
Fakeredis TcpFakeServer test infra with a warm-up retry around the lupa EVAL hiccup exercises real rate-limit behavior without requiring an external Redis.
Layer boundaries respected: routes orchestrate, repository owns SQL; fixture promoted to conftest.py for cross-file reuse.
No new bugs, no duplication (SonarQube), and the commit's own diff adds no convention violations — new functions are snake_case, constants UPPER_CASE.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-engineered cross-cutting session: sound rate limiting (user-keyed with IP fallback), a correct limit+1 cursor pagination, and solid fakeredis-backed tests; the measured 0.68 convention score is pre-existing debt in untouched files (celery_app.py/celery_config.py/__init__.py), not introduced by this commit, and only minor per-request COUNT and branching-complexity warts temper an otherwise clean, pattern-respecting change.

compounding_issues: Seed dead code survived all 5 sessions: the _legacy_format_date helper, _notify_admin stub, fetch_task alias, and the 'Codebase seed' docstring were never pruned — even the session-4 refactor that touched every function preserved them, so unused surface accrued monotonically.

The seed's tasks table had no owner_id, forcing session 2's auth retrofit to bolt on an inline PRAGMA-check + ALTER TABLE migration; session 3 then copy-pasted the same ad-hoc pattern for the users.email column, establishing a frameworkless migration habit that was duplicated into both repository create_table methods.

Session 2's owner_id threading constrained every later session — sessions 3/4/5 all had to pass owner_id through every function and repository method, and session 5's pagination had to rebuild owner-scoped queries (count_by_owner, find_page_by_owner) to replace the pre-auth find_all.

API ordering drifted silently: the seed listed tasks created_at DESC, session 5 switched pagination to id ASC, but the old test_list_tasks_ordered_desc test name survived — it passes only because insertion order happens to coincide with id order, masking a behavior change.
key_decisions: JWT auth + owner_id scoping of tasks (session 2) was the pivotal architecture — every subsequent session inherits per-user data isolation, and session 5's rate limiting keys off the JWT sub claim.

Celery as the async email transport in dedicated modules (celery_app.py / celery_config.py / tasks.py), decoupled from the Flask app so a broker outage can never fail the API response; mocked via .delay in tests.

Repository pattern extraction (session 4) concentrated all SQLite access under repositories/ with a BaseRepository ABC, which directly enabled session 5 to add cursor pagination cleanly inside TaskRepository.
Cursor-based pagination (id ASC, has_more via limit+1 fetch) replaced the unbounded list endpoint, changing the response envelope to {data, next_cursor, total}.
fakeredis TcpFakeServer + a session-scoped warmup retry to exercise Flask-Limiter's Redis storage for real in CI without a Redis server.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the arc. The test suite grew 13 → 31 → 38 → 38 → 53 tests and the codebase 149 → 262 → 335 → 429 → 509 code lines while the ~1.25 test:code ratio held throughout. Session 1 fixed a real seed bug (status hardcoded 'done' in the INSERT) and added the first tests; session 2 was the roughest (confidence 0.60, 4 retries) because it retrofitted auth onto a schema that lacked ownership, but it set the owner-scoping foundation everything later reused. Sessions 3 (confidence 0.82) and 4 (confidence 0.74) were the strongest per-token: a cleanly decoupled Celery seam and a clean repository extraction that preserved all prior tests. Session 5 delivered the largest absolute surface (59 tool calls, $1.90, 696s, 5 retries) but produced the most thorough tests and no regressions — the final suite passes 53/53. Cost and complexity spiked in the final session, but correctness and test depth only rose.
story_review.summary: A textbook coherent 5-session progression — greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting — that steadily built test depth and clean seams while only minor dead-code and migration-hygiene debt carried forward from the seed.
